problems.description: 74 naming violations across source files (index.ts, ExamplePlugin.ts, cache.ts): classes/interfaces not PascalCase, functions not camelCase, constants not UPPER_CASE; measured convention score 0.56.
SonarQube reports +40 cognitive complexity for only 2 new functions — the greenfield logic is already over-complex at session 1.
+1 bug introduced in a fresh scaffold; the CLI bin targets dist/src/cli.js implying a build step whose output isn't part of this scaffolding.

strengths: Clean, atomic greenfield commit: jest.config.js + lockfile establish the test harness up front.
Standard TypeScript layout (src/ + tests/) with explicit ts-jest testMatch and clearMocks.
Runtime deps (gray-matter, marked) are well-chosen for a static site generator; engine pinning via package.json.
commit_reviews.summary: Sound session-1 scaffolding that is architecturally reasonable and pattern-consistent, but static analysis flags 74 naming violations and +40 cognitive complexity in the (diff-truncated) source files — the visible diff alone looks cleaner than the 0.56 convention score suggests, so the debt likely concentrates in cache.ts/ExamplePlugin.ts/index.ts.

problems.description: Adds two competing template engines (ejs AND handlebars) in one feature_addition session while retaining the existing rendering path, creating redundant template-dispatch routes instead of one engine abstraction. Consistent with the +24 cognitive complexity and +5.9% duplications in the SonarQube delta.

Convention score 0.56 with 74 violations, predominantly naming rules (PascalCase/camelCase/UPPER_CASE) across new/changed files including ExamplePlugin.ts, index.ts, and cache.ts — the agent did not match the project's established naming conventions.
SonarQube delta reports +1 smell and +24 cognitive complexity from the dual-engine selection/rendering logic, making the build path harder to follow than the single-path design it replaced.

package-lock.json churn reclassifies handlebars and transitives (minimist, neo-async, picocolors, source-map, uglify-js, wordwrap, balanced-match) from devDependencies to production, doubling the runtime dependency surface; necessary for a runtime engine but amplified by shipping two engines at once.
The visible diff covers only package manifests and src/cli.ts wiring; no test additions are evident for the new template engines (though the diff is truncated, so this could not be fully verified).

strengths: Feature is on-task for the story's feature_addition phase — template support is a natural extension for a static site generator.
CLI wiring is threaded through existing module boundaries via the ssg export surface (DEFAULT_TEMPLATES_DIR imported from './ssg'), respecting the established file structure.
package.json and package-lock.json are kept in sync, and the change introduces no new bugs (bugs +0) with +5 functions added.
commit_reviews.summary: The commit delivers a plausible template-engine feature but over-engineers it by shipping two competing engines on top of the existing path (driving +24 complexity and +5.9% duplication) and drops convention adherence to 0.56 with 74 naming violations, leaving net negative technical debt.

problems.description: 74 SonarQube naming violations (Sonar convention score 0.56) across index.ts, ExamplePlugin.ts, cache.ts: classes/interfaces not PascalCase, functions not camelCase, constants not UPPER_CASE.
Cognitive complexity jumped +48 across only +6 new functions — the integration logic concentrates too much branching/indirection per function and should be decomposed.

Visible hunk adds chokidar + ws (+@types/ws, +14 imports) to package-lock.json with no package.json hunk shown; if the manifest wasn't updated in the truncated portion, lockfile and package.json are out of sync. Also verify whether chokidar belongs in devDependencies if only the dev server uses it.

detectOpenHandles: true in jest.config.js is sensible given the new ws server, but it can make CI flaky if any handle legitimately stays open — ensure WebSocket/file-watcher handles are closed in teardown.
Duplication increased +0.9% on top of the naming and complexity issues, slightly reducing maintainability of the new integration code.

strengths: Live-reload integration uses purpose-built, idiomatic dependencies (chokidar for FS watching, ws for WebSocket push) rather than reinventing them.
Adding detectOpenHandles proactively guards against async leaks introduced by the new websocket/file-watcher server.
Feature is scoped coherently to a single integration concern (+2 files, +6 functions) and extends via a plugin pattern (ExamplePlugin.ts) instead of hardcoding.
Lockfile update is internally consistent: chokidar's transitive deps (anymatch, braces, fsevents, etc.) were correctly moved from dev-only to shared, reflecting the new runtime path.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-scoped live-reload integration for the SSG using idiomatic deps, but a net regression on code quality driven by 74 TypeScript naming violations and a +48 cognitive-complexity jump.

problems.description: build() and buildAsync() duplicate the full pipeline orchestration (onStart→beforeBuild→onFile→afterBuild→onEnd) in sync and async variants, doubling the maintenance surface of the engine core (consistent with SonarQube smells +7).

The engine never populates ctx.pages: readPages()/sortPages() in src/markdown.ts are never wired into SSGEngine, so the onFile loop iterates an empty array and the build is non-functional integration.

Convention score 0.56 with 74 violations across the new files (PascalCase classes/interfaces, camelCase functions, UPPER_CASE constants flagged in index.ts, ExamplePlugin.ts, cache.ts) — a refactor session should not be lowering conformance.
plugin-loader.ts monkey-patches require.extensions['.ts'] as a global side effect for every import, mutating process-wide Node behavior rather than scoping the transpile.
Cognitive complexity +45 for a refactor — the duplicated orchestration and loadConfig/resolveConfigPath/normalizeConfig/loadTsModule chain add branchiness in the loader path.

strengths: Well-defined plugin lifecycle hooks (onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd) give an extensible, idiomatic plugin-pipeline architecture for the SSG.
Duplications down 1.7% and zero new bugs per SonarQube; clean module separation between engine, loader, markdown, and plugins.
Typed Plugin/PluginContext interfaces and per-hook method signatures keep plugin authoring type-safe (ExamplePlugin implements the full contract).
commit_reviews.summary: The commit establishes a sound hook-based plugin architecture, but for a 'refactor' session it regresses: convention adherence is low (0.56, 74 violations), the engine never actually loads pages (empty-pages pipeline), and duplicate sync/async build paths add 879 lines and +45 cognitive complexity.

problems.description: templateHashFor() and indexTemplateHash() in cache.ts duplicate near-identical logic for composing template/layout/partial sources (matches duplications +2.0% measurement); extract a shared hashing helper parameterized by the template key.

Cognitive complexity +54 in the build path (buildWithStats) — the incremental/clean/skip branches create a deeply nested decision surface; consider decomposing the run into smaller phases (reconcile cache, render, persist).

Measurement flags cache.ts for 'Interfaces/Classes should use PascalCase', but the new interfaces (CacheEntry, BuildCache, BuildStats) are already PascalCase and no classes are declared — suggests the analyzer is reporting either pre-existing violations or noise; the introduced code itself appears convention-clean.
No test coverage added for the new cache module (load/save/prune/hash logic); the corrupt-cache fallback path in loadCache() is exactly the kind of edge case worth a unit test.

strengths: Incremental builds are a well-scoped, natural feature for an SSG and are cleanly isolated in a dedicated cache.ts module rather than tangled into the render engine.
Hash-based invalidation correctly covers both source and template/layout/partial artifacts, with pruneCacheEntries() handling stale pages and a version field guarding against schema drift.
Graceful degradation: loadCache() returns null on missing/corrupt caches, and --clean provides an explicit escape hatch.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped incremental-build feature that fits the SSG architecture and respects existing patterns, though the +54 cognitive complexity and duplicated template-hash logic warrant refactoring; note the mechanical 0.56 convention score appears partly driven by pre-existing files since the new cache.ts is itself PascalCase-compliant.

compounding_issues: Session 2 implemented BOTH Handlebars and EJS template engines when the spec allowed either; the dual-engine dispatch plus parallel render paths (renderPage vs renderPageWithTemplates) added +24 complexity and 5.9% duplication that persisted through S4/S5, forcing template-hash logic to cover both engines.

The seed Express Todo API (root index.ts) was never deleted or replaced across all 5 sessions; it remains as dead code at HEAD, and its naming violations appear to keep the mechanical convention score pinned at 0.555 in every commit, distorting the per-session quality signal.

Session 4's refactor introduced duplicated sync/async build paths (build vs buildAsync with two separate run loops), and Session 5 then had to thread its cache logic through both paths, leaving duplicated template-hash computation (flagged by the S5 review).
Cognitive complexity accumulated monotonically (+40, +24, +48, +45, +54); even the designated refactor session increased complexity (+45, smells +7) rather than paying it down.
Session 3 (dev server) flailed: 1334s runtime, 3 retries, required a continuation, and produced ~11 throwaway test files (chok/min/min2..minD) before converging — the costliest session at $0.065.
key_decisions: Modular greenfield foundation: gray-matter + marked with comment-delimited frontmatter, a typed Page interface, and clean parse/read/sort/build separation, all documented with JSDoc.
Dual-engine template support (Handlebars + EJS) selected by file extension in Session 2 — flexible but over-engineered.
chokidar-based live-reload dev server exposed via `ssg serve` in Session 3.

Hook-based plugin architecture (onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd) with a PluginPipeline, runtime TS plugin loader (ssg.config.ts + plugins/ExamplePlugin.ts), and ssg.ts reduced to a facade re-export module in Session 4.
Incremental builds via a .ssg-cache.json content+template-hash manifest threaded through the PluginContext in Session 5 — built directly on Session 4's plugin seam.
Leaving the unused seed Express API in root index.ts rather than removing it during the greenfield session.
story_review.trajectory_description: The story starts strong: Session 1 delivers a clean, well-documented SSG core (parse markdown, render pages, CLI) with all tests green, then quality dips through the middle — Session 2 over-engineers the template layer, Session 3 is a costly and flailing dev-server integration, and Session 4's plugin refactor is architecturally ambitious but lands as a net regression (duplicate sync/async paths, +45 complexity, reviewed 'worse'). Session 5 reverses the trend: the incremental-build/caching feature is the best-scoped commit, adds the most tests (6 passing), earns a 'better' review, and directly validates the Session 4 architecture by threading cache state through the plugin pipeline. Throughout, every session's test suite stays green and complexity climbs monotonically, so the final product is a coherent, functional, plugin-based SSG that improved in architecture late even as code-complexity metrics degraded steadily.
story_review.summary: A logical 5-session arc (core → templates → dev server → plugin refactor → incremental caching) with strong bookends but a mid-run quality dip driven by early dual-engine over-engineering and a complex, never-cleaned-up refactor that only gets redeemed by the well-scoped final cross-cutting session.
